lines: Ever wonder why a chill makes your skin sprout tiny hills?
When you’re cold or scared, smooth muscles called arrector pili contract.
They’re activated by the sympathetic nervous system, the fight‑or‑flight driver.

beats.title: What the bumps do
lines: The hair lifts, trapping a thin air layer for warmth.
In many animals the puffed‑up fur also makes them look bigger, scaring off threats.

beats.text: Humans keep this reflex despite little hair.
lines: It’s a leftover from our furry ancestors.
So we get goosebumps from cold, fear, awe, or a powerful song.
Next time a stirring song gives you chills, watch the skin on your forearm and feel the tiny bumps appear.

sources.claim: Arrector pili muscles contract via sympathetic nervous system
Hair standing traps air for insulation and makes animal appear larger
Goosebumps persist in humans as a vestigial reflex triggered by cold, fear, awe, music
